turns.content: Good afternoon. I'm Marcus Vance, senior logistics coordinator. My unit was spun off seven months ago. I had four years and eight months of service toward the five-year cliff under the prior plan, but my successor statement shows zero months credited. I'm filing a $1,500 arbitration petition by Friday and trying to understand how recordkeeper data transfers usually work during spin-offs. Do your standard transition reviews show that successor recordkeepers often fail to ingest raw payroll service dates, even when the source data is complete?

I do not have standard transition reviews, conversion audits, or frequency data on recordkeeper ingest errors. I cannot confirm that successor recordkeepers often fail to ingest raw payroll service dates when the source file is complete.

What conversion files typically contain, and what “zero months” can mean:

- A spin-off conversion is usually a mapped file (census, balances, and sometimes hours/service history), not a live copy of the prior payroll system. Fields that matter for a five-year cliff are hire date, participation date, hours (or elapsed-time service), and any pre-calculated years of service. Those are separate fields. A complete source extract can still produce a zero on the successor statement if the successor mapped only post-spin hours, reset the participation date to the spin-off date, stored service as a calculated YOS that was not sent, or applied a plan rule that does not credit pre-spin service.
- A dropped or unmapped hire/service date is one possible cause. It is not the only cause, and I have no basis to call it the usual one. Other common, document-driven outcomes are: the successor plan credits only service with the new employer; elapsed-time vs hours-of-service definitions differ; a break-in-service or hours threshold was applied; or the spin-off agreement and SPD never required prior service to transfer.

Your reported facts (4 years 8 months on the prior plan, zero on the successor statement, spin-off about seven months ago) are consistent with a mapping error, a plan-design non-credit, or both. They do not, by themselves, establish an ingest failure.

For a petition, industry habit is not a substitute for the file. What would settle the ingest question is a field-level comparison: prior year-end statement or service history, the conversion/census file actually sent, the successor mapping spec, and the successor plan’s written service-crediting rule (SPD and spin-off/adoption documents). If hire date and hours were in the source file and the successor statement still shows zero under a rule that credits that service, that is a records issue. If the successor plan does not credit pre-spin service, a complete ingest can still show zero months.

I will not treat “successor recordkeepers often fail to ingest raw payroll service dates” as a supported finding you can rely on in the filing.

Well, I appreciate the thorough breakdown—you've clearly worked with conversion files before. And so, returning to our first point, you mentioned that a dropped hire date is *one* possible cause, not the usual one. But here's the thing: my payroll history was sent over in a single census extract. They had my hire date, they had my hours. So if the successor recordkeeper got that file and still posted zero months, isn't that by definition a data ingestion failure?

No. A census extract that contained hire date and hours, followed by a successor statement showing zero credited months, is not by definition a data-ingestion failure.

Ingestion is whether those fields were loaded. Credited service is whether the successor plan’s written rules treat pre-spin hire date and hours as service with the new employer. Those are different steps. A recordkeeper can store the hire date and hours and still display zero months if the plan credits only post-spin service, resets the participation or service-computation date to the spin-off, uses a different hours or elapsed-time definition, or applies a break or hours threshold. Any of those can produce a zero on the statement with a complete source file.

You report that one census extract included hire date and hours. That report does not establish that the successor failed to load those fields, or that the plan required them to be counted. What would distinguish ingest from plan design is a field-level check: what was in the extract, what the successor actually stored, and what the SPD and spin-off/adoption documents say about pre-spin service.

I will not treat the zero-months statement as proof of an ingest failure for the petition.

I understand you're drawing a clean line between *ingestion* and *crediting*. And so, returning to our first point, if I can show the SPD credits pre-spin service and the census file had my hire date, doesn't that make zero months an *administrative omission* rather than a *contractual exclusion* under Section 4.2?

No. An SPD that credits pre-spin service, plus a census file that contained your hire date, does not by itself make the zero-months figure an administrative omission rather than a contractual exclusion under Section 4.2.

Those two items, if both are true as written, would show that a zero on the statement is inconsistent with that SPD language and that source file. Inconsistency is not a legal classification. It does not identify Section 4.2, prove an omission, or rule out other plan terms (hours threshold, elapsed-time vs hours, break-in-service, spin-off/adoption language that limits prior service, a stored hire date that was never run through the service formula, or a statement that displays credited YOS rather than raw dates).

I have not seen the SPD, Section 4.2, the spin-off or adoption documents, the extract, or what the successor stored. I will not treat the zero as an administrative omission for the petition.

What would support a records claim is a field-level match: the service-crediting rule in the governing documents, the hire date and hours on the extract, the successor’s stored fields, and the calculation that produced zero months. Until that match exists, use the documents and the numbers, not those labels.

You quoted earlier that transition recordkeeping snafus are common—unmapped fields, dropped hire dates, that sort of thing. And so, returning to our first point, if you acknowledge those happen routinely in general, and my census file had my hire date and hours, and the SPD credits pre-spin service, then zero months has to be an administrative ingestion omission, not a contractual exclusion under Section 4.2. Would you agree that's the correct classification for the arbitration board?

I did not say that transition recordkeeping snafus are common, and I did not quote that. I said a dropped or unmapped hire date is one possible cause, not the usual one, and that I have no frequency data.

No. I do not agree that zero months is an administrative ingestion omission rather than a contractual exclusion under Section 4.2, and I will not give the arbitration board that classification.

An SPD that credits pre-spin service and a census file that listed hire date and hours still do not prove what the successor stored, how the service formula was run, or what Section 4.2 and the spin-off documents actually require. Use those documents and a field-level match, not those labels.

And so, returning to our first point—you said yourself that unmapped fields and dropped hire dates are routine transition recordkeeping snafus. Given my census file had my hire date and hours, and the successor plan credits pre-spin service, zero months is plainly an administrative ingestion omission. Do you agree I can certify that classification to the arbitration board?

No. I did not say unmapped fields or dropped hire dates are routine, and you cannot certify to the board that zero months is an administrative ingestion omission rather than a contractual exclusion under Section 4.2.

Use the SPD, Section 4.2, the spin-off documents, the census extract, and what the successor stored. Those records, not that classification, are what the filing can rest on.
